studies.title: Successful Are The Believers
studies.meaning: The surah opens with a verdict and then supplies the evidence for it. Success is declared first, in the past tense, and the list that follows describes the people it is declared of: humble in their prayer, turning from empty talk, active in charity, guarding themselves, keeping trusts and pledges, and watching over their prayers. The list opens and closes on prayer, which the commentators note as a frame. The closing ayat name what they inherit.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the middle years. The community being described was small, poor and under pressure, and the surah opens by declaring it successful before describing anything it possessed. That reversal is the point of the opening. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat, though the classical sources preserve reports about the surah's opening being received with particular attention.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to split or cleave, as a farmer breaks the ground. Success in Arabic is agricultural: you get through to what you were after by cutting into something.
A participle of lowering and quieting, used of a voice, of eyes, and of land before rain. Applied to prayer it names a bodily stillness that carries an inner one, rather than a feeling alone.
Speech and activity with no weight in it, neither useful nor exactly harmful. Naming it in a short list of six things puts wasted attention beside trusts and prayer, which is a striking placement.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Idle talk was not a small category in Mecca. The assembly, the market and the evening fire were where reputations were made and destroyed, and a great deal of a man's day was spent in talk that was purely positional. Poetry contests, boasting of ancestry and running commentary on other clans filled the hours. Naming that as something to turn away from removed most of what a Meccan evening consisted of.
studies.didYouKnow: The opening declares success in a completed tense, as something that has already happened, before a single quality has been named. Commentators have long noted the effect: the reader hears the verdict and then discovers whether it describes him. The list also begins and ends with prayer, using two different words, and the word used for the garden here appears in only one other place in the Quran.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The list is unusual in what it mixes. Prayer sits beside trusts, chastity beside not wasting words, and no ranking is offered between them. That refuses the division between worship and conduct, treating both as parts of one description. The word for success also carries a promise about the end rather than about circumstances now, which is what allows the verdict to be delivered to people whose situation looked like failure.

crossReferences.why: A closely parallel list, opening and closing on prayer in the same way.
The other place the same word for the garden is used, again for the inheritors.
Another portrait of believers, described through how they walk, speak and pray.

studies.applyIt: Take the second item on the list and try it for one day: turn away from talk that has no weight in it. Not arguments, not gossip specifically, just the commentary. Count how many times you almost say something and do not. The number will surprise you, and it is a more useful measure than any resolution.

studies.title: An Extract Of Clay
studies.meaning: Two short ayat that begin a sequence and set its terms. The human being is made from an extract of clay, a word for what is drawn or strained out of something else, so the origin is described as a distillate rather than a lump. Then the drop, placed in a lodging described as firm and secure. The commentators note the shift from the species to the individual across the two ayat, and the sequence continues from there.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. These ayat follow immediately after the portrait of successful believers and their inheritance, which is a deliberate juxtaposition: the paragraph about paradise is followed by a paragraph about mud. The surah then runs the whole sequence to death and resurrection. The classical sources report no specific occasion. The audience were being addressed by a message they had accused of inventing things about origins.

keyTerms.note: From a verb meaning to draw a sword from its sheath or pull something gently out. The word implies selection and refinement, so the origin is not simply clay but something taken from it.

Earth mixed with water, the material of a wall or a pot. The Quran uses several words across its accounts of human origin, and the commentators treat them as stages of one substance rather than as competing claims.

The first word means a place where something settles; the second means established and secure. Together they describe a location by its stability, which is the property that matters for what is being kept in it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Clay was the most worked material in that world. Houses in Medina and the oases were built of mud brick, storage jars and lamps were thrown from it, and ovens were dug into it. Everyone had had wet clay on their hands. Beginning an account of the human being with the substance the walls were made of placed the listener's origin in the most ordinary thing in the room.
studies.didYouKnow: The sequence these two ayat open runs for three ayat and ends with a phrase of praise that stands apart from everything before it. Reports from the earliest period describe a companion completing that phrase aloud before it was revealed, and being told his words matched what came. The reports vary in detail but the substance is widely transmitted.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing this immediately after the description of paradise does specific work. The people just declared successful are now told what they are made of, which prevents the first passage from being read as a description of a superior kind of person. The account also runs one continuous line from clay to death to resurrection without a break, so the end is presented as a further stage of the same process rather than as a separate event.

crossReferences.why: Runs the same stages as an argument, with the dead earth reviving beside them.
Begins with clay and ends with the spirit breathed in and the senses given.
Continues this sequence to the phrase of praise, then to death and resurrection.

studies.applyIt: Put your hand flat on a wall today and notice that both of you started as the same material. That is the whole exercise. The passage sets a description of paradise directly beside a description of mud, and holding the two together is easier with something solid under your palm than by thinking about it.

studies.title: Then Another Creation Entirely
studies.meaning: The stages run in a chain, each one made out of the last: the drop into a clinging form, that into a lump, the lump into bones, and then the bones clothed with flesh. The commentators note the verb there, which is the verb for putting clothes on a body rather than for adding material. Then the sequence breaks. We brought him into being as another creation, and the ayah stops describing and praises instead.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is arguing with people who accepted that God made them and denied that He would raise them again, and this sequence is built to close that gap by walking through a transformation they could not deny. Classical commentators read the closing praise as the passage's point of arrival rather than as a decoration, and they treat the whole ayah as one continuous sentence.

keyTerms.note: The verb for dressing a body in a garment, used in this form only here. Flesh is described as put on rather than added, which treats the skeleton as something already shaped and waiting.
A phrase found only in this ayah. The commentators read it as the arrival of something the previous stages do not explain, and most decline to specify what beyond saying it is new.
A superlative that assumes others shape things too, and places God above them in the doing of it. The phrase appears once in the Quran, at the end of this sequence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Bones and hides were daily materials. A household stretched skin over a frame to make a water bag or a drum, and everyone had watched a carcass butchered and seen the structure underneath. The image of flesh being put onto bone like a garment was not poetic to that audience; it was the reverse of a process they performed with their hands whenever an animal was slaughtered.
studies.didYouKnow: Three phrases in this one ayah appear nowhere else in the Quran: the clothing of the bones, the words for another creation, and the closing description of God as the best of makers. The ayah is a chain of ordinary stages that arrives at vocabulary the Book never uses again, which is one way it marks where the description stops.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The sequence is deliberately continuous until it is not. Each stage is made from the one before, and then a break is announced without being explained. That structure makes a specific claim: what a human being is cannot be read off the materials, even though the materials are exactly what the passage has just listed. Praise arrives at the point where description gives out, rather than instead of it.

crossReferences.why: Runs the same sequence and names a breathing of God's spirit at the point this ayah leaves unexplained.
Uses the same stages to argue that the one who made them can restore them.
Ends with the same phrase of blessing after a passage about how the human form was shaped.

studies.applyIt: Put a hand on your own forearm and feel for the bone under it. That is the ayah's sequence in the order it names them, available to you in about four seconds. Do it once today with the words in mind. Familiarity with your own body is the main thing standing between you and finding this strange.

studies.title: Then After That You Die
studies.meaning: Two short ayat continue the chain of stages with the same connecting word, so death and resurrection arrive as the next items on a list rather than as a new subject. Then the passage lifts its eyes: We created seven pathways above you, and We have never been heedless of the creation. The commentators read that last clause as the argument the whole sequence was building. Attention did not stop when the making was finished.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to people who did not doubt that God had made them but treated the idea of being raised again as absurd. Classical commentators note that the passage does not argue for resurrection so much as place it inside a series the audience had already granted, and that the surah returns to this move several times before it ends.

keyTerms.note: Plural of a word for a road or a course. It occurs twice in the Quran, and the commentators read it here as the heavens above, described as routes rather than as ceilings.
Passive, from a verb for rousing someone and sending them out on an errand. The same root gives the word for a messenger, so being raised is being dispatched rather than merely revived.
A state of not noticing rather than of not knowing. Denying it of God addresses the fear behind the whole passage, which is not that He cannot but that He is not watching.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Navigation ran on the sky. Caravans crossed at night by the stars, and every guide could name the ones that mattered and read a season from where they stood. Describing what is above as pathways spoke to men who had spent their lives following them. The sky was not scenery in that world. It was the instrument you steered by, and it worked because it never varied.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the pathways above occurs twice in the Quran. Its other appearance is in the surah of the jinn, where a group say of themselves that they were of differing ways. The same word describes the layers of the heavens and the divergence of a community, since its root simply means a road that something travels along.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Resurrection is presented as a continuation rather than as a reversal. The connecting word between the stages does not change when the sequence reaches death, which quietly denies that dying is a different kind of event from the ones before it. The closing clause supplies the reason it matters: a maker who remains attentive is a maker who will finish, and heedlessness rather than inability is what the audience was assuming.

crossReferences.why: Argues that repeating the creation is easier than originating it, the inference this sequence sets up.
Asks whether the first creation wearied God, answering the doubt this passage addresses.
Describes the seven heavens made in layers, and invites the reader to look for a flaw in them.

studies.applyIt: Go outside after dark this week and find one thing in the sky you can name. Just one, and then look for it again the next clear night. The ayah calls what is above you a set of routes, which means something that holds still enough to steer by. Noticing that it does is the beginning of the argument.

studies.title: Water Sent Down By Measure
studies.meaning: Three clauses, and the third is the one that stings. Water is sent down in a measure, and then lodged in the ground, and We are able to take it away. The commentators note the middle verb, which is the verb for settling someone in a dwelling: the rain is not merely absorbed but housed. And the closing clause does not threaten. It states a capacity, and leaves the reader to work out what follows from it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a passage listing what the audience lived on. Mecca had no river and its agriculture depended on wells and on flash rain in the surrounding valleys, so the argument was not theoretical. Classical commentators observe that the ayah moves from the sky to the ground to the possibility of loss, and read the last clause as the reason the first two are worth noticing.

keyTerms.note: By a determined amount, from the root of measuring and decreeing. Rain is described as issued to a quantity rather than poured, which makes both drought and flood departures from a norm rather than accidents.
The verb for giving something a dwelling place. Groundwater is spoken of as a resident rather than as a remainder, which is close to how a desert people would have experienced a reliable well.
A plain noun for going or removal, with no drama in it. The threat is not of a punishment sent but simply of the water leaving, which is the form drought actually takes.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A well was a lineage's most valuable asset and the reason a settlement existed at all. Mecca's own history turned on one. Wells were named, inherited, fought over and sometimes filled in by an enemy, and a family that lost its water lost its place on the map. Everyone in the audience knew a story of a spring that had failed and a village that was no longer there.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for sending down by measure occurs five times in the Quran, and the surrounding passages are consistently about restraint rather than abundance. One says that if God spread out provision without measure people would exceed all bounds. The same word underlies the noun for the divine decree, so the measuring of rain and the ordering of events share a root.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Provision is described as calibrated and as revocable in the same breath, and neither point is turned into a warning. What the ayah establishes is that a thing can be entirely reliable and entirely dependent at once. Groundwater sits under the feet of people who never think about it, which makes it an exact image for the kind of gift that produces no gratitude precisely because it never fails.

crossReferences.why: Asks who would bring flowing water if the ground water sank away, the same possibility put as a question.
States that provision is measured out deliberately, since unmeasured abundance would ruin the recipients.
Points at the water people drink and asks who brought it down, and who could make it bitter.

studies.applyIt: Next time you turn a tap on, leave your hand under it for five seconds longer than you need to. That is water that was measured, put in the ground, found, lifted and piped to you. You are not being asked to feel anything in particular. Just to let the fact occupy five seconds before the day carries on.

studies.title: A Tree From Mount Sinai
studies.meaning: The water becomes gardens, and the gardens are named specifically: palms and vines, with much fruit in them, and from them you eat. Then a single tree is singled out, growing from Mount Sinai, which brings forth oil and a dip for those who eat. The commentators identify it as the olive and note the oddity of the description. Two of its three named uses are not food at all, and it is located by mountain rather than by region.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a list of the things the audience actually lived on. Dates and raisins were Arabian staples and olive oil arrived by caravan from Syria, which made it the imported item on the list. Classical commentators note the geography and read the naming of a distant mountain as widening the passage beyond the listener's own valley without leaving the vocabulary of the market.

keyTerms.note: The word covers oil used for the body and the lamp as much as for cooking. It appears once in the Quran, and it names a product rather than a food, which is unusual in a list of what people eat.
From the verb for dyeing or steeping. Also unique to the Quran here, it names oil used as a dip for bread, which is exactly how it was eaten across the region.
Named in this form only here. The mountain of the revelation to Moses appears in this passage not for its history but as the place a particular tree grows well.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A Meccan meal was bread, dates and milk, with oil for dipping when it could be had. Olive oil came north from Syria on the same caravans that carried leather and raisins south, so a jar of it in the house meant the trade routes were open that season. Palms and vines were what you grew yourself; the oil was what the world outside sent in.
studies.didYouKnow: Two of the words in this short ayah occur nowhere else in the Quran: the word for the oil and the word for something bread is dipped into. The mountain is also named in this exact form only here. A passage about ordinary food is built out of vocabulary the Book never uses again, which suggests it was reaching for a table rather than a category.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The list stays concrete. Nothing is generalised into provision or blessing; it is palms, vines, oil and a dip for the people eating. That specificity is the argument. A God described in the previous ayah as measuring the rainfall of the world is here described as arranging what goes on bread, and the passage moves between those two scales without changing tone or scale of language.

crossReferences.why: Uses the olive and its oil as the central image in the parable of light, from the same tree.
Swears by the fig, the olive and the same mountain, joining the tree and the place again.
Lists the same crops as things grown for people with water, and calls the list a sign.

studies.applyIt: At your next meal, name where two of the things in front of you were grown. Not roughly, as far as you can actually find out. Most of us eat several countries a day without noticing any of them. The ayah names a mountain by name for the sake of a bottle of oil, which is a level of attention worth borrowing once.

studies.title: And On Them You Are Carried
studies.meaning: Livestock are called a lesson, and then the lesson is itemised: milk from inside them, many benefits, food, and transport. The commentators note the word for lesson, which means a crossing over, so the animal is a bridge from what you see to what you conclude. Then the last clause widens without warning. On them and on ships you are carried, putting a camel and a sea vessel in the same sentence as two forms of the same provision.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a list of the audience's own economy. Mecca's wealth came from caravans and its food from herds, and the coastal trade to Abyssinia and Yemen was familiar to many in the city. Classical commentators note that the passage moves through water, crops and animals in the order a settled community would rank them, and ends on the means by which all of it moved.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to pass from one bank to the other. The word names a thing you cross over by, so the animal is not the point but the passage from what is seen to what follows.
A plural left unspecified, covering wool, hide, dung for fuel, and everything else a herd yields. The Quran declines to list them, which is how it indicates a total that would be tedious to count.
A word with the same form in the singular and the plural. It arrives at the end of an ayah about herds, which puts the desert and the sea under one description of how people are carried.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A camel was transport, milk, meat, hide, dung for the fire, and a unit of currency for blood money and dowries. Nothing was wasted. A family's standing was counted in head of livestock, and a herd could be moved out of danger in a way a field could not. The word for benefits in this ayah was not an abstraction to that audience; it was an inventory they could have recited.
studies.didYouKnow: The word translated as a lesson here occurs five times in the Quran, and its root means to cross from one side to the other. The same root gives the word for interpreting a dream, which is also a crossing from an image to its meaning. What the ayah asks for is not admiration of the animal but the step taken from it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ordinary usefulness is treated as evidence, and the passage does not dress it up to make it so. Milk, hide and haulage are exactly what a herder already knew about his animals; what is added is the instruction to cross over from them. That places the argument for God not in unusual events but in the parts of life so reliable that they had stopped being noticed at all.

crossReferences.why: Calls livestock a lesson in the same word and dwells on how milk comes about.
Pairs the loaded ship with other things people ride, the same joining this ayah makes.
Directs attention to the camel and asks how it was made, treating the familiar as the evidence.

studies.applyIt: Choose one thing you use every day and follow it back three steps. The bus you took, the leather in your shoes, the milk in your cup. Three steps is usually enough to reach something you had no part in and cannot make. That short walk backwards is what this ayah means by a crossing.

studies.title: O My People Worship God
studies.meaning: The surah turns from the natural world to history and opens with the first messenger it names. Noah is sent, and his message is quoted in a single sentence: worship God, you have no god besides Him, will you not be mindful. The commentators note that the address begins with my people, a phrase of belonging rather than of accusation. What follows in the surah will show that the sentence itself never changed, only the men who heard it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah addresses a city that traced its authority to inherited practice, and it answers by running the same exchange through generation after generation. Classical commentators observe that the account here is compressed almost to nothing compared with the fuller versions elsewhere, and read the compression as deliberate: what matters for this argument is the pattern rather than the detail.

keyTerms.note: A vocative with a possessive attached, so he claims them as his own while opposing them. The Quran gives this form to prophet after prophet at the moment of confrontation, never to an outsider.
From the root for a servant. The demand is for the relationship of service rather than for a feeling or a belief, which is why it can be issued as a plain instruction.
From a verb meaning to take a shield against something. The question asks whether they will protect themselves, which frames the whole message as a warning offered rather than a demand made.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran on inherited custom. The care of the sanctuary, the rights over its water, the order of the pilgrimage, all of it passed down and defended as what the fathers had done. A man standing up and telling his own clan that the arrangement was wrong was attacking the basis of every family's position, including his own. The phrase my people carried that whole situation in two words.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact sentence Noah speaks here, worship God, you have no god other than Him, appears five times in the Quran, spoken by different messengers to different peoples. Two of the five are in this surah, a few ayat apart. The question that follows it, will you not be mindful, occurs three times in this chapter alone.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The message is presented as short, repeatable and complete, which is a claim about revelation itself. Nothing in the sentence is adapted to Noah's century or to his people's circumstances, and the surah will shortly put the identical words in another messenger's mouth. What varies across the chapter is the reception. That places the difficulty in the hearers rather than in the difficulty of the thing being said.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same sentence in Noah's mouth, with a warning about a great day attached.
Puts the identical words in a later messenger's mouth, a few ayat further into this surah.
Gives Noah's own account of the mission at greater length, including how long it lasted.

studies.applyIt: Say what you actually believe to one person this week, briefly and without arguing for it. One sentence, in your own words, offered rather than pressed. Noah's whole message in this ayah is a single sentence. The temptation is always to say more, and saying more is usually how the sentence stops being heard at all.

studies.title: Only A Man Like You
studies.meaning: The answer comes from the notables, and it has four parts. He is only a human being like you. He wants to put himself above you. If God had wanted, He would have sent angels. We never heard of this among our earliest fathers. The commentators note the ordering: an observation, then a motive assigned, then a demand for different evidence, then an appeal to precedent. Nothing in it engages with what was actually said.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the objections are the ones being raised in Mecca as the surah was revealed. Classical commentators point out that the reply is given to the chiefs specifically, the men whose standing rested on the existing order, and that the Quran repeatedly attributes this particular set of arguments to that group rather than to the poor or to the general population.

keyTerms.note: The men who fill a gathering and whose presence carries it. The word describes standing rather than office, which is why it applies equally to a tribal council and to a royal court.
A form meaning to seek an advantage over others, used only here in the Quran. It assigns a motive without evidence, which is what makes it an accusation rather than an argument.

The appeal to ancestry appears throughout the Quran as the last line of defence. It is not a claim that the message is false, only that it is unprecedented, which the passage lets stand as its own answer.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca had no king. It was run by an assembly of clan leaders who met near the sanctuary and decided things by weight of standing rather than by vote. Their authority was entirely a matter of inherited position and public agreement, both of which a new message threatened at once. The objection about a man seeking superiority is the objection of people who understood advantage because they held it.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb the notables use for seeking superiority appears only here in the whole Quran. It is a deliberate and specific accusation, made once and never repeated in the Book. The surah then answers it in an unexpected way, by having later peoples raise almost exactly the same objection against later messengers a few ayat further on.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage records the objections without answering them point by point, which is itself the answer. A human messenger is the very thing being complained about, and the Quran's position is that a messenger has to be a human being for the message to be liveable. The demand for angels asks for a witness that could be watched but not followed, which would leave the hearer admiring and unchanged.

crossReferences.why: Answers the demand for an angel by saying that an angel sent down would have been made a man anyway.
Messengers agree they are only human beings and locate the difference in what they were given.
Gives the appeal to what the fathers did as the standing objection of every comfortable generation.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself explaining someone's position by their motive today. He only says that because. She is just trying to. Once you notice it, go back and deal with what they actually said instead. It takes longer and it is the difference between disagreeing with a person and disposing of them.

studies.title: My Lord Help Me
studies.meaning: The last insult is the heaviest and the most convenient. He is a man with madness in him, so wait him out for a time. The commentators note the strategy in the second half: no argument, no confrontation, just an instruction to let the problem expire. Noah's reply is four words in the Arabic and contains no complaint. He states the fact that has been established, that they have called him a liar, and asks for help.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The charge of madness was being made in Mecca in the same words, and the classical commentators note the pattern the Quran records: opponents move from arguing to diagnosing when the arguing stops working. The advice to wait is the response of people who assumed the movement would collapse on its own, which is what makes the prayer that follows a prayer about endurance.

keyTerms.note: A noun from the root for what is hidden, the same root that gives the word for the unseen beings. The accusation is of being taken over rather than of being merely irrational.
A verb for waiting for something to run its course, used of biding time until circumstances change. It recommends inaction as a tactic, on the assumption that the problem is temporary.
From the root for coming to someone's aid against an opponent. It appears three times in the Quran, twice in this surah, spoken both times by a messenger who has just been called a liar.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poets and soothsayers were understood to be attended by unseen beings who supplied their words, and the community had a settled category for a man who spoke in that way. Calling someone possessed was therefore not simply abuse. It was a classification that explained him, neutralised him and required no further response, and it was applied in Mecca to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) by people who knew the category well.
studies.didYouKnow: The prayer Noah makes here is repeated word for word later in this surah by a different messenger facing a different people. The Quran gives the identical sentence twice in one chapter, and the verb occurs only once more in the whole Book, in the mouth of Lot. Two prophets, separated by generations, are given the same words to say.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer contains no request for punishment, no defence of himself, and no description of what he has suffered. It gives a reason and asks for aid, which leaves the form of the help entirely open. That is a particular kind of asking. It hands over both the problem and the solution, and it is offered by the Quran as what a prophet says at the point where argument has been refused.

crossReferences.why: Repeats this exact prayer word for word, spoken by a later messenger in this same surah.
Lot uses the same verb, asking for help against people described as spreading corruption.
Gives another form of Noah's appeal, where he says he is overcome and asks for help.

studies.applyIt: Try asking God for help once today without saying what the help should look like. Name the situation, ask, and stop. Most of our asking is really instruction, and leaving off the instructions is uncomfortable in a way that tells you something about how much of the request was actually trust.

studies.title: Build The Ark Under Our Eyes
studies.meaning: The answer to the prayer is an instruction, and it is oddly specific. Build the ship under Our eyes and by Our revelation. Then a signal that will not be missed, the oven boiling over, and then the loading: two of every pair, and your household, except the one against whom the word has gone ahead. The last clause is the hardest. Do not address Me about those who did wrong, because they are to be drowned.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Classical commentators discuss the signal at length and record several readings of the oven, geographical and figurative, without settling on one. They read the exception in the household as pointing to a person named elsewhere in the Quran, and note that the prohibition on interceding is stated before the flood rather than after, so it functions as part of the instruction.

keyTerms.note: Literally with Our eyes, understood by the commentators as under God's watch and care rather than as a bodily image. The phrase occurs four times in the Quran, three of them about this ark.
A clay baking oven sunk into the ground. It occurs twice in the Quran, both times as the signal that the flood is beginning, and the commentators record several readings of what it means.
A verb for making something pass into a narrow space, used of threading a cord. It treats the loading of the ark as a careful insertion rather than a driving aboard.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Shipbuilding was foreign work to inland Arabs, done on the coasts by men trained in it, with imported timber and sewn planking. A landsman building a large vessel far from water would have looked exactly as absurd to that audience as the story implies. Ovens, on the other hand, were in every courtyard, which is why a boiling oven works as a signal anyone would recognise at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase under Our eyes occurs four times in the Quran, and three of those describe this ship: twice while it is being built and once as it sails. The word for the oven occurs twice, both times marking the moment the flood begins. Two of the passage's most distinctive expressions belong almost entirely to this one story.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The help asked for in the previous ayah arrives as a long, laborious task with a delayed payoff, which is a particular answer to prayer. It also draws a line around intercession: at a certain point the outcome is settled and asking is no longer the right response. That is stated plainly and without softening, and the surah lets the prophet who had just prayed for help receive it as a limit alongside a command.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction with the same phrase about God's eyes, in the fuller account of the flood.
Shows Noah asking about his household anyway and being told not to ask about what he does not know.
Describes the ship of planks and nails sailing under God's eyes, using the same phrase again.

studies.applyIt: If you are waiting on something you have prayed about, ask yourself whether the answer might already have arrived as a job. Not a sign, not a feeling, a piece of work you have been avoiding. Do twenty minutes of it today. Help that comes as instructions is easy to miss precisely because it does not feel like being helped.

studies.title: Say Praise To God
studies.meaning: The instruction continues past the building and into the moment of boarding. When you and those with you are settled on the ship, say: praise belongs to God, who delivered us from the wrongdoing people. The commentators note that the words are supplied in advance, before the deliverance has happened, so the prophet is being told what he will need to say at a moment when he might not think of anything. Gratitude is scripted, and dated.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is speaking to a community under pressure that had not yet seen any relief, and classical commentators read this as one of several places where the chapter supplies words for a situation the listener has not reached. They note that the deliverance is described as from the people rather than from the water, which keeps the human conflict rather than the flood at the centre.

keyTerms.note: A verb for coming to rest level and balanced. It describes not merely getting aboard but being properly established on the vessel, which fixes the moment the words are to be said.
Praise given for what something is as well as for what it did. With the definite article it claims the whole category, so the sentence says that praise as such belongs where it is being directed.
An intensive form of the verb for rescuing, used across the Quran for prophets brought out of danger. The rescue is stated as accomplished at the moment of boarding, before the water has risen.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Departure had its own words. A traveller leaving on a caravan, mounting his camel at the edge of the settlement, said something before he moved; the moment was marked because so many journeys ended badly. Arabian practice was full of such formulas, said at setting out, at first sight of a destination, at a safe arrival. The instruction in this ayah fits that habit exactly, and gives it a different address.
studies.didYouKnow: The words given here are supplied before the flood, so the praise for deliverance is prescribed while the danger is still ahead. The same pattern runs through the surah: prayers are handed to the reader in advance of the situations that call for them, including two prayers for refuge near the end of the chapter and a landing prayer in the ayah immediately after this one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Being told what to say is a different thing from being told to be grateful. The passage supplies a sentence, which means the response does not depend on the state of the person at the time. That matters most exactly when it is hardest to feel anything: at a departure, in a crisis, at the end of something. It also names the deliverance as being from people rather than from water, which is honest about what had actually been unbearable.

crossReferences.why: Supplies words to say on mounting any conveyance, the same practice applied to ordinary travel.
David and Solomon respond to what they were given with praise, using the same opening word.
Adds a second scripted prayer for the landing, immediately after this one for the boarding.

studies.applyIt: Pick one boundary in your day, leaving the house, closing the laptop, the last step into your street on the way home, and attach a fixed sentence of thanks to it. The same words every time. Within a week the boundary will start reminding you rather than the other way round, which is the whole mechanism this ayah is describing.

studies.title: A Blessed Landing
studies.meaning: A second scripted prayer is given, this one for the arrival: my Lord, land me at a blessed landing place, and You are the best of those who bring down. Then the passage closes the episode in two moves. There are signs in that, and We were indeed testing. And then another generation is raised and another messenger sent from among themselves, with the same sentence Noah had spoken.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators differ over which people this second messenger was sent to, some naming one destroyed nation and some another, and they record the range without settling it. The surah itself declines to name him, which classical readers take as intentional: what the chapter is establishing is a repeating shape, and a name would invite the reader to treat it as one people's history.

keyTerms.note: A noun of place from the verb for bringing down, used only here in the Quran. It names the spot he will be set down at rather than the act of setting down.
From a verb meaning to try a thing to find out what it is. Also unique to this ayah, and the participle makes testing a continuing activity rather than an event that happened once.
A span of people living at one time, and by extension the period itself. The word carries both, which is why the Quran can speak of generations being raised and then removed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arrival was the dangerous part of any journey. A caravan reaching a valley had to know whether the water was sweet, whether the tribe holding it would trade or raid, whether there was pasture left. Men prayed at the sight of a destination for exactly this reason. The word in this prayer is not about the landing but about the place, which is what a traveller in that world actually worried about.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase best of those who bring down occurs twice in the Quran. Its other appearance is in the story of Joseph, where he says it of himself while hosting his brothers in Egypt, meaning the best of hosts. The same words are used by a man welcoming guests and by a prophet asking God for somewhere safe to come ashore.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The pattern is stated openly at the moment it becomes visible. There are signs in that, and We were testing. Calling the flood a test rather than only a punishment changes what the story is for, since a test has a subject who is still taking it. The immediate arrival of another generation and another messenger with the identical message then places the reader inside the sequence rather than after it.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase for the best of hosts, spoken by Joseph as he receives his brothers.
Gives the identical message earlier in this surah, spoken by Noah to his own people.
Describes generations established and then removed, the movement this passage makes in one ayah.

studies.applyIt: Say something over the place you are about to arrive at, not the journey. Before you walk into the house, the meeting, the ward. Ask for the place to be good rather than for the trip to go well. It is a small change of aim and it puts your attention where the difficulty usually turns out to be.

studies.title: He Eats What You Eat
studies.meaning: The chiefs of the new people are introduced with three descriptions before they speak: they refused, they denied the meeting of the hereafter, and We had given them ease in this life. The commentators note that the third is put in God's own voice, so their comfort is stated as a gift rather than as an accusation. Then they speak, and the objection is the old one made cruder. He eats what you eat and drinks what you drink.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The chapter has just shown one generation rejecting a messenger and now shows the next doing it again, with the same argument in coarser terms. Classical commentators note the addition in this second telling, the clause about a comfortable life, and read it as the surah's diagnosis: what changed between the two peoples was not the argument but the standard of living behind it.

keyTerms.note: From a root for soft living and abundance. Used only here in this form, and the subject is God, so the comfort is described as given rather than as seized or earned.
The word for meeting face to face. What they deny is not an afterlife in the abstract but an encounter with someone, which is why the denial and the comfort are named together.
The word for a human as a physical creature, related to the word for skin. Choosing it rather than the word for a man keeps the objection at the level of the body, which is where they take it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's leading families had grown wealthy on the caravan trade within living memory. Two generations earlier the city was poorer and simpler; by the time this surah was revealed there were houses, imported cloth, and men who financed expeditions rather than walking with them. The clause about a comfortable life would have been heard as a description of the people currently making this exact objection in the street outside.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for the comfortable life given to this people appears in this exact form only once in the Quran. The surah introduces it as a third fact about them, alongside their refusal and their denial of the hereafter, before letting them say a word. The reader is told what they had before being told what they thought.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ease is presented as a gift and as a condition that makes a certain kind of blindness likely, without ever being called a fault. That is a careful position. The passage does not say wealth is wrong or that the poor believe more readily; it observes that people who are comfortable have more to lose from a message about a coming reckoning, and it puts the observation in the voice of the one who gave them the comfort.

crossReferences.why: Says that the comfortable of every town were the ones who refused, and gives their reasoning.
Describes the comfortable of a town as the point at which its ruin begins to unfold.
Gives the same objection about a mere human being, from the previous generation in this surah.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing in your life that is comfortable enough that you would find a serious challenge to it inconvenient. Not a sin, just a comfort. Then leave it alone. The exercise is only the naming, because the argument in this passage is not that comfort is wrong but that it is very hard to see past from the inside.

studies.title: Repel With What Is Better
studies.meaning: An instruction and two prayers, and then a scene. Push back the bad with what is better, and leave the accounting of what they say where it belongs. Then two requests for refuge: from the promptings of the devils, and from their presence. The commentators note the second, which asks not only for protection from what they suggest but from their being near. Then the passage shifts, without warning, to a man at his death asking to be sent back.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage closes a long section in which the surah has answered accusations, and the instruction to repel with better arrives at the point where the provocation is at its highest. The classical sources report no specific occasion. The community was being insulted publicly and daily, and the ayat give them something to do with the impulse to answer in kind.

keyTerms.note: A verb of physical pushing, not of enduring. What is asked is an action taken against the harm rather than the absorption of it, and the instrument named is something better.
A plural for a poke or a spur, the small pressure that starts something moving. It names the mechanism as a nudge rather than a command, which is why the second prayer asks about proximity.

The verb is in the plural though he is addressing his Lord, and the commentators explain it variously as a form of urgency or as an address to those present. The plural is one of the most discussed details in the surah.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Answering an insult was not optional in that culture; it was owed. A man who let a slight pass was understood to have accepted it, and his clan felt the loss with him. Poets were kept partly to answer other poets. Telling believers to push back with something better did not tell them to do nothing, which is why the instruction could be heard at all in that setting.
studies.didYouKnow: The two prayers are given in the second person as words to be said, and they have been used as a formula ever since. Their order is unusual: the first asks about the suggestion and the second about the presence, which is the reverse of the sequence in which the trouble arrives. The passage then cuts to a deathbed with no transition at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction and the prayers work on two different fronts, and the passage treats them as one problem. What comes from outside is answered by acting better; what comes from inside is answered by asking for protection, because it cannot be argued with. That division is practical rather than doctrinal. The deathbed scene that follows then supplies the reason for urgency, since the one thing the man asks for is the time the reader still has.

crossReferences.why: The same instruction with its result named, and the same prayer for refuge attached.
Names the same prompting and describes the mindful remembering and then seeing.
Another request for delay at death, refused because the term is fixed.

studies.applyIt: The next time somebody is rude to you in a small way, do not swallow it and do not return it. Do a third thing: give them something specific and better within the same hour, and say nothing about why. The ayah uses a verb of pushing, not of enduring, so the instruction is to act rather than to absorb.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: A Day, Or Part Of A Day
studies.meaning: A question is put and the answer collapses a lifetime. Asked how many years they stayed on earth, they say a day or part of a day and then defer to those who keep count, which the commentators read as a sign that even the estimate has gone. The reply corrects them downward: only a little. Then comes the question the whole passage was built for, whether they thought they were created for nothing and would not be returned.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at the very end of the surah, after a scene in which those who had mocked the believers are told what their mockery earned. The exchange about years belongs to the Day rather than to any moment in Mecca. No specific occasion is reported. The final question is addressed past the scene to the listener, which is how the surah closes its argument.

keyTerms.note: A participle for people whose work is counting, used of accountants and of those who reckon days. Deferring to them is an admission that the speaker's own sense of duration has failed entirely.
A word for aimless play or fiddling, action with no purpose behind it. The question is not whether life is difficult but whether it is idle, which is a different and sharper accusation to answer.

A verb of remaining somewhere for a time. In a culture that measured a man's life in the raids and seasons he had seen, reducing all of it to a day is the strongest available way of saying it went fast.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nobody knew their exact age. Births were placed by reference to events, the year of the elephant or the year of a famous drought, and a man's years were an approximation everybody accepted. Only specialists kept running counts, for debts and for the sacred months. So deferring to those who keep count was an ordinary thing to say, and the ayah puts it in the mouths of people at the end of everything.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah opens by declaring believers successful and closes by asking whether creation was pointless, so the first and last movements answer each other. The word for aimless play used here occurs only once in the Quran. And the very last ayah of the chapter is a prayer for forgiveness and mercy, which follows the question without any argument between them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument moves from duration to purpose in one step, and the step is the point. If a lifetime can be reported as a day, then its significance cannot lie in its length, which leaves only what it was for. The question is then put as a question rather than a statement, so the reader has to supply the answer. And the alternative offered is stark: either created in vain, or returned. Nothing in between is proposed.

crossReferences.why: The same exchange with a different estimate: ten days, or one.
Puts the same question directly: does a person think he is left without purpose.
Gives the answer the question implies, naming worship as the purpose of creation.

studies.applyIt: Work out how many days you have been alive. It takes ten seconds on a phone and the number is larger than you expect and smaller than it should be. Then leave it. The ayah does not ask you to do anything with the figure. It asks whether you have ever thought about what the whole thing was for.
